title: Mohini Dey Opens NDTV Summit, Carrying Indian Roots Onto Global Stage
excerpt: The 29-year-old bassist opened the NDTV World Summit 2026 in New Delhi and told the broadcaster she feels fortunate to be born in India — a profile built on a childhood bass, Carnatic rhythm and a global touring career.
body:
• Bassist Mohini Dey opened the NDTV World Summit 2026 with a song she wrote as a child, then performed tracks including The Dey Way and A.R. Rahman's O Humdum Suniyo Re.
  • The 29-year-old told NDTV on the sidelines of the summit that she feels fortunate to be born in India, and spoke about losing her father.
  • Mumbai-born Dey was given a bass at age three by her father Sujoy Dey, performed on stage at ten, and was working with Ranjit Barot by eleven.
  • Her playing now spans Rahman's band, Willow Smith's touring crew, the Dhurandhar soundtracks and her band MaMoGi.

Bassist and composer Mohini Dey opened the NDTV World Summit 2026 in New Delhi with a song she wrote as a child, before taking the stage with her band to perform tracks including The Dey Way and A.R. Rahman's O Humdum Suniyo Re, according to NDTV's summit coverage. Speaking to NDTV on the sidelines of the summit, the 29-year-old musician talked about her love for music, supporting her family through her passion, losing her father, and why she feels fortunate to be born in India. It was a home-stage moment for a musician whose career is now largely international — and who, in detailed profiles, has repeatedly traced that career back to her Indian upbringing.

Context

Dey was born in Mumbai to two musicians: her father Sujoy Dey, a studio bassist, and her mother Romia, a Hindustani classical singer. In a profile published by Hindustan Times, she said she did not choose the bass herself: "My dad chose it for me. I [was] three years old when he first put a bass guitar in my hands." Her father built a small wooden guitar for her hands, and she recalled that music was constant at home: "I don't think I ever experienced music as something separate from life. It was just always there." Bass Magazine, in its own profile, records the same start — a first lesson on her father's Fender Jazz Bass at age three, an onstage appearance at ten, and teenage work with mentors including drummer Ranjit Barot, keyboardist Louis Banks and Rahman after she set aside plans to study fashion design. Hindustan Times puts the milestones in sequence: accompanying Barot on tour at eleven, playing with Zakir Hussain at thirteen, and performing with Rahman's band on Coke Studio at sixteen, while juggling school with practice, rehearsals and performances.

Impact

That early training produced a style that draws directly on Indian rhythm. Hindustan Times reported that Dey stunned Berlin's Sonic Pluriverse Festival when she broke into konnakol, a Carnatic form of vocal percussion, during a rock performance with her band MaMoGi, and that listeners recognised her bass immediately on the Dhurandhar 1 and 2 soundtracks released in 2025 and 2026, including on Ishq Jalakar. She released her self-titled debut solo album in 2023, joined Willow Smith's touring band after Smith found her through that album, and has performed with Steve Vai and opened for Childish Gambino and Coldplay, according to Hindustan Times. Bass Magazine noted that she tours out of Nashville, where she records sessions for clients around the world from her home studio, while stating plainly where home remains: "India will always be my home because my mom and sister are there." Dey herself framed the connection in musical terms to Hindustan Times: "For me, it's never been about trying to fit into a global sound. It's about bringing my identity into the music, my upbringing, the way I hear rhythm, the way I phrase things." The summit conversation also touched on loss. Dey reconnected with her father before he died in 2023, after a three-year estrangement that began when she moved out at seventeen, Hindustan Times reported. She credited him with her career: "He gave me his all, including my gift. He was my creator."

What's Next

Hindustan Times reported that Dey's second album was due for release and that she was touring Asia, Europe and the United States, while continuing to share rhythm and improvisation techniques with her more than 934,000 followers on Instagram. Her summit opening puts that trajectory in front of a policy and business audience in New Delhi rather than a concert crowd: a Bengali, Mumbai-born bassist, trained by her father and by Indian classical and film-music mentors, presenting Indian-rooted music as the opening note of a global summit. For Dey, by her own account, the roots are not a theme she visits for such occasions — they are the foundation she says she carries into every room she plays.
